notes.text: Before Eli — That is, under his inspection and direction. Word - The word of prophecy, or the Revelation of God's will to and by the prophets. Precious - Rare or scarce, such things being most precious in mens' esteem, whereas common things are generally despised. Open vision - God did not impart his Mind by way of vision or Revelation openly, or to any public person, to whom others might resort for satisfaction, though he might privately reveal himself to some pious persons for their particular direction. This is premised, as a reason why Samuel understood not, when God called him once or twice.
His place — In the court of the tabernacle.
Went out — Before the lights of the golden candlestick were put out in the morning.

Did not know — He was not acquainted with God in that extraordinary or prophetical way. And this ignorance of Samuel's served God's design, that his simplicity might give Eli the better assurance of the truth of God's call, and message to Samuel.

Came and stood — Before, he spake to him at a distance, even from the holy oracle between the cherubim: but now, to prevent all farther mistake, the voice came near to him, as if the person speaking had been standing near him.

glossa.text:
*The lamp.* ((ID.)) Which burned in the tabernacle before the light of day. For under the light of day it was quenched, but it shone until the morning; or this signifies that Heli should remain in blindness until he were utterly quenched together with his offspring, that is, should die.

But mystically the blindness of Heli signifies the blindness of the Jews, who acknowledged not the Saviour present, nor the brightness of his miracles, nor his teaching, until the priesthood together with the people and the temple was overthrown.

notes.text: Afar off — Thou knowest what my thoughts will be in such and such circumstances, long before I know it, yea from all eternity.
Compassest — Thou discernest every step I take. It is a metaphor from soldiers besieging their enemies, and setting watches round about them.
Beset me — With thy all-seeing providence. And laid - Thou keepest me, as it were with a strong hand, in thy sight and under thy power.
I cannot — Apprehend in what manner thou dost so presently know all things.

glossa.text: *Unto the end, a psalm of David* *Ddvid**.* ((CASS.)) A psalm full of the depth of mysteries, etc., *as far as* veiled in the prophets, manifest in the Gospel. ((AUG.)) The whole Christ speaks, as one entire man, etc., *as far as* as two in one flesh. *Lord, thou hast proved me.* ((CASS.)) First, concerning the knowledge of God, etc., *as far as* fourthly, how the wicked do him no hurt, there, *If thou wilt kill, O God,* etc. *Lord, thou hast proved.* ((AUG.)) Now restored in Jerusalem, etc., *as far as* this is the person of the whole of human nature returning.

*Thou hast understood.* ((CASS.)) The foreknowledge of the Godhead is here shown, etc., *as far as* because the manhood assumed cannot be made equal to the divine substance. *From afar off.* ((AUG.)) While I am still on pilgrimage, before I come to the fatherland, as the father ran to meet the younger son returning, because he understood his thoughts from afar off, because he had said within himself, worn out with want *egestare*: *I will arise and go to my father.*

*My path,* namely the evil one, by which I went, forsaking my father.

*And the line.* (Otherwise) the boundary, how far I came: far indeed had I gone, but thou wast there. He speaks as a fugitive caught, the vengeance of God following after him.

*And all my ways:* before I went in them; and thou didst permit me to go in labour, that I might return if I would not labour: this I confess. *For there is no guile in my tongue:* now I have justified in thy grace.

My *last things,* when I fed the swine, *The old things,* when I asked for the portion of the substance: this according to the parable. But mystically, *The old things,* when through the ancient sin *pecatum* we fell: *The last things,* the penalty, when we came into this mortality, which is the last, if we are willing to return; otherwise the eternal remains. *Thou hast formed me,* unto labours, unto which we are all born. *Thou hast laid.* (Otherwise) Thou hast made heavy the hand, the avenging hand, weighing down the proud man wholesomely, that it may raise up the humble man, in the hand made heavy.

*Wonderful,* and incomprehensible *incomprehensibllis* to me. *Thy knowledge is become.* It is not easy for me to contemplate thee, whom in my pride I forsook, as it was before, when I was with thee, when I said, give me the portion of the substance. *From me,* that is, from my sin.

*It is strengthened,* (otherwise) it has prevailed. *And I shall not be able* to attain to it of myself. ((AUG.)) In Exodus it is read that the Lord, etc., *as far as* I am not hidden from thee, whose boundary thou seest.

notes.text: All things — Which are lawful for you. Are lawful for me, but all things are not always expedient - Particularly when anything would offend my weak brother; or when it would enslave my own soul. For though all things are lawful for me, yet I will not be brought under the power of any - So as to be uneasy when I abstain from it; for, if so, then I am under the power of it.

As if he had said, I speak this chiefly with regard to meats; (and would to God all Christians would consider it!) particularly with regard to those offered to idols, and those forbidden in the Mosaic law. These, I grant, are all indifferent, and have their use, though it is only for a time: then meats, and the organs which receive them, will together moulder into dust. But the case is quite otherwise with fornication. This is not indifferent, but at all times evil. For the body is for the Lord — Designed only for his service. And the Lord, in an important sense, for the body - Being the saviour of this, as well as of the soul; in proof of which God hath already raised him from the dead.
Gen. ii, 24.
But he that is joined to the Lord — By faith. Is one spirit with him - And shall he make himself one flesh with an harlot?

Flee fornication — All unlawful commerce with women, with speed, with abhorrence, with all your might. Every sin that a man commits against his neighbour terminates upon an object out of himself, and does not so immediately pollute his body, though it does his soul. But he that committeth fornication, sinneth against his own body - Pollutes, dishonours, and degrades it to a level with brute beasts.

And even your body is not, strictly speaking, your own even this is the temple of the Holy Ghost — Dedicated to him, and inhabited by him. What the apostle calls elsewhere "the temple of God," chap. iii, 16, 17, and "the temple of the living God," 2 Cor. vi, 16, he here styles the temple of the Holy Ghost; plainly showing that the Holy Ghost is the living God.

Glorify God with your body, and your spirit — Yield your bodies and all their members, as well as your souls and all their faculties, as instruments of righteousness to God. Devote and employ all ye have, and all ye are, entirely, unreservedly, and forever, to his glory.

glossa.text: *All things are lawful to me.* Because he said that it was rather to be borne than that causes should be ill conducted, lest anyone should think that his own goods are in no way to be reclaimed, he subjoins: It is lawful for me to reclaim all my own, but yet I will not reclaim them, because not all things are expedient for my course, but hinder it. Again he shows the same by another reason. As if: They are lawful, but I will not reclaim them, because, since I am free, I do not wish to be brought under a judge's own power *suo potestate*; read *sub potestate* — the plate prints *sub* in the parallel clause on the same line: or, I do not wish to be under the dominion of any thing, so as to offend a brother for its sake.

*Meat for the belly.* For these reasons they are not to be reclaimed, nevertheless meat is due to the belly. By these understand the necessaries of nature, and therefore it is lawful for them to be reclaimed. But there must not be much labour for these, because they will be destroyed, and therefore it is lawful either that judgment be made concerning them, or that it be passed over.

*Your bodies.* It cannot be that a body is not holy, which the sanctified Spirit uses. *They are the members,* etc. As all the members which are ruled by one and the same soul are one body, so all who are quickened by the same Holy Spirit are made one body in Christ. *Of Christ.* Because he took a body, and is the head of bodies.
*One body.* Natural philosophers hand down that they are so united that, if their blood were mingled, it would be wholly joined together.

*But he that is joined,* etc. Not by identity of substance, but by participation, since he who here draws near by faith so cleaves to him that he is a partaker of his beatitude, which will then be full, when his desire will be satisfied in unchangeable goods, namely in the Trinity itself, his Lord, whose image he is.

*Fly fornication.* With other vices a conflict may be awaited, but flee this one, that you come not near it, because it cannot otherwise be better conquered. *For every sin.* No sin so dishonours and defiles the body as that one. *But he that committeth fornication.* It is not said on account of the greatness of fornication, that it alone is in the body, and the others outside the body. For many are as great as fornication, or greater. But on account of the quality, because it defiles the body more basely than other sins.

*The temple.* From this it is plain that the Holy Spirit is God; for if he were not God, he would assuredly not have ourselves for a temple. But not only the Holy Spirit, but the Father also and the Son have us for a temple. The temple therefore of God, that is, of the whole Trinity, is the holy Church.

*And bear God.* To bear God is to show the image of God in deeds well done. *In your body.* If thou sparest not thyself for thine own sake, spare at least for God's sake, who has made thee a house for himself. And if thou overthrowest it, thou sinnest against God, which is a grave kind of sin; but it is another kind to sin against man.

notes.text: Jesus of Nazareth — So Philip thought, not knowing he was born in Bethlehem. Nathanael was probably the same with Bartholomew, that is, the son of Tholomew. St. Matthew joins Bartholomew with Philip, Matt. x, 3, and St. John places Nathanael in the midst of the apostles, immediately after Thomas, chap. xxi, 2, just as Bartholomew is placed, Acts i, 13.

Can any good thing come out of Nazareth? — How cautiously should we guard against popular prejudices? When these had once possessed so honest a heart as that of Nathanael, they led him to suspect the blessed Jesus himself for an impostor, because he had been brought up at Nazareth. But his integrity prevailed over that foolish bias, and laid him open to the force of evidence, which a candid inquirer will always be glad to admit, even when it brings the most unexpected discoveries. Can any good thing - That is, have we ground from Scripture to expect the Messiah, or any eminent prophet from Nazareth? Philip saith, Come and see - The same answer which he had received himself from our Lord the day before.
Under the fig tree I saw thee — Perhaps at prayer.

Nathanael answered — Happy are they that are ready to believe, swift to receive the truth and grace of God. Thou art the Son of God - So he acknowledges now more than he had heard from Philip: The Son of God, the king of Israel - A confession both of the person and office of Christ.

Hereafter ye shall see — All of these, as well as thou, who believe on me now in my state of humiliation, shall hereafter see me come in my glory, and all the angels of God with me. This seems the most natural sense of the words, though they may also refer to his ascension.

glossa.text: *Into Galilee, and he found Philip.* Galilee is interpreted transmigration, or revelation. For man passes over from the vices to the virtues, and afterwards from virtue to virtue, and so revelation is made to him, that the God of gods may be seen in Sion. About to call a disciple therefore to follow him, that is, to imitate him, he goes out into Galilee, intimating by the place itself that, as he himself advanced in wisdom, and as through sufferings he entered into glory, so also do his followers.

*From Bethsaida the city.* Not in vain is the city named, nor in vain is it said to be the city of Philip, of Peter and of Andrew. For it sounds *house of hunters*, in which is marked the disposition and the office of these men: for they are hunters in the taking of souls; whence Philip, before he becomes an apostle, of his own accord calls Nathanael.

*Philip findeth,* etc. Nathanael, most skilled in the Scriptures, understands what others do not, namely, that from Nazareth there comes forth a singular Nazarene; but because he was most learned, he was not chosen into an apostle: for all the apostles were first from the unlearned, that the wise might be confounded. *Whom Moses wrote of.* Like a wary hunter he builds up the truth for his brother by many reasons, namely, that Jesus is he who is foretold in the law and the prophets. The son of Joseph, who is of the house of David: so that through him (not that he was born of him), together with Mary his mother (whom he knew from the prophets to have brought forth as a virgin), he may be marked as being of David.

*And Nathanael said to him.* Either he asks in doubt, or he affirms, as one skilled in the law, that from a city of so great a name there can be some good man, or an outstanding teacher, or the supreme Saviour. For Nazareth is interpreted flower, or bud of cleanness, or holiness. And to either utterance there is fittingly subjoined: *Come and see,* etc.

*Behold an Israelite indeed.* Guile, that is, dissimulation. For if he has sins, he confesses them. He does not therefore deny him to be a sinner, but praises the confession in him. But the Pharisees are guileful, who proclaim themselves good when they are evil.

*Whence knowest thou me?* Knowing that the Lord speaks of his conscience, he asks not out of indignation, but in wonder: whence, and from what power. *I saw thee under the fig tree. ((AUG.))* Nathanael, that is, the gift of God, is the true people of Israel, the gift of God, which was hidden under the fig tree, that is, made subject under the habit of sinning and the shadow of death, as the first parents covered themselves under the leaves of the fig tree; where he had been seen and sought by the Lord before he saw and sought the Lord, and even before he called him through the apostles.

*Rabbi, thou art the Son of God.* Because Nathanael knew that Christ, though absent, had seen what he himself had done in another place, that is, how and where he was called by Philip, which is a token of Deity, he confesses him not only master, but also the Son of God, and king of Israel, that is, Christ: in which he is proved to be an Israelite, as it is said, that is, one seeing God.

*You shall see heaven opened.* Nathanael the Israelite is said to be about to see heaven opened, and the angels of God descending and ascending, as of old the patriarch Jacob saw the ladder, and the angels ascending and descending, who through the blessing was called Israel. *The angels of God.* Often this miracle appeared, that angels ascended and descended upon Christ. *Upon the Son of man.* Christ calls himself the Son of man, affirming what is less, namely his humanity; Nathanael and Peter call him the Son of God, which is greater, affirming his divinity. Behold the confirmation of either nature in Christ. These, confessing his deity, deserve to ascend; he, asserting his humanity, testifies that he came to redeem. *Upon the Son of man.* He confirms that he is man, lest any should err, believing him to be only God, as even Peter did when he said: *Far be it from thee, Lord.*

registers.label: Spare
lines: The boy Samuel heard his name in the night.
Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.
You have searched me and known me, O God.
You knew my words before I spoke them.
Jesus said: come and see. I saw you.
Where the world overlooks us, you know us by name.
Come, let us worship the God who calls.
Speak, Lord, your servant is listening. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: In the night, when the lamp of God had not yet gone out, a voice called a boy by name — and called, and called again.
Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.
O Lord, you have searched me and you know me; you knit me together, you trace my path, you know my sitting down and my rising up.
Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.
Jesus saw Nathanael under the fig tree before anyone introduced them, and said simply: come and see.
Speak, Lord, your servant is listening.
So we come, already known and already called, and we open our ears to the One who names us.
Speak, Lord, your servant is listening. Amen.
